speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset of this Parliament, at this particularly poignant period in our history, we should be committing ourselves to the kind of future greatness that our combination of peoples and nature makes possible-a greatness whose character rests neither on numbers nor on power, but on the quality of life we make possible for all those who live within our borders.
At this moment in particular, then, our goal must not be merely the temporary patching up of immediate flaws or grievances that we find in the land; our goal should be nothing less than the setting out of objectives which will enable us a decade from now not only to look back and say that Canada is
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
indeed more decent in its arrangements and more exciting for all its members, but is indeed still one country because of the things we started to do in 1980.
We in this Parliament, Madam Speaker, have an obligation to the people of Canada to provide the leadership and policies that will make this reality possible. We must do so not only because that is what a democratic mandate ought to be about in general, but because as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) recognized, particularly at this moment, such policies, such actions, are necessary to garner and maintain support among all our regions and peoples which is so essential to Canada at this time.

Quebeckers will have to vote on the political future of their province and of Canada on May 20. They have two possibilities: sovereignty-association and Canada. Quebeckers will say Yes to Canada if they think that we want deep changes and that we reject the status quo. Like other Canadians but more strongly, they demand changes in Quebec. In this session, they expect us to act. It would not be enough to insist on the economic benefits offered by Canada to convince Quebeckers, but at the same time I want to stress that it is not enough to have taken action. It is also necessary to convince them that we want fundamental changes to build a society that is more just for everyone in Canada.

The Speech from the Throne and the Prime Minister have suggested certain laudable goals that might take us in this direction. The Prime Minister focused in a serious and thoughtful way on some of the abstract principles involved in a Oui or Non vote on the question that is before the people of the province of Quebec, and in a general, abstract way on some of the considerations that are involved in developing a sense of loyalty or patriotism in the regions.
There are some matters he did not touch upon which I think are so central to the argument, so important to the reality of genuine feelings of national unity, that I intend certainly to touch upon them, because the argument cannot be left in abstract form. If we learned anything from the recent debate in the province of Quebec on the question before that assembly, we should be convinced that logic, and reason, while having an important role to play, are quite inadequate in terms of winning the hearts and minds of a people to move in a certain direction in history.
O)
Therefore, Madam Speaker, I want to put my argument in somewhat recasted form to deal with the framework that the Prime Minister provided for the argument. When we talk about patriotism and about a sense of fairness being connected, as the Prime Minister suggested, that we are likely to be patriotic and have a sense of the legitimacy of the whole of our country if we have a sense that fairness is in fact occurring where we happen to live, in our work place or in our region,
38

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
then I will agree with that part of the argument because it is one that we in this party have made for a long time.
But through you, Madam Speaker, I want to ask the Prime Minister to consider his own throne speech in the context of that framework, to reflect a bit upon our recent history when he was Prime Minister and to make some judgments about the accuracy of his own statement today that his own government, through its actions, had moved in rather decisive ways to create feelings of patriotism and feelings of fairness in these regions. In my view, the problems singled out in the throne speech-that of foreign ownership, that of the need to have improvements for women in Canada, that of the need for an industrial strategy-are all problems that are not new in Canada, in fact, they are not new in the sense of being addressed by the government that we have today.
Canadians know that in reality we do not have a new government today. What we have is the same Prime Minister and the same party that has continuously governed for 12 years except for a nine-month interlude. Canadians know that the programs enunciated in the Speech from the Throne are in fact being enunciated in the Speech from the Throne precisely because of the inadequacy of the government that we had for the past 12 years, and that it was the Liberal government itself that created the need for its own throne speech yesterday.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I ask the Prime Minister to reflect on his own speech when he says that patriotism is related to a sense of a fair deal, and to ask himself how the people of the various regions of Canada who are considering this very important and historic debate today are going to respond to that when they think about his own government.
How are they going to respond to the promises when they consider the following: that it was a Liberal government that created its own problem of a lack of a sense of patriotism, to use the Prime Minister's words, or a feeling of "the enemy within" to use his phrase applied in a new context. For example, Madam Speaker, if you were a western Canadian on the prairies in the last few years and you did not get a commitment for the speedy implementation of the Hall royal commission, and because you did not there was prolonged alienation from western farmers who had a sense of grievance that was not being dealt with by the Liberal party, how would you feel? Or if you were a Cape Bretoner in Sydney in the last six, seven, eight, or nine years and you knew you had the potential steel resources, the coal and the labour force, but you had a central government that failed to address the needs of the people and the human reality of getting stable jobs that could have been provided by serious capital investment in the steel industry that only the national government and not the government of Nova Scotia could provide, then how would you feel about such a situation? How are people going to feel toward a government now that talks about doing something for an industrial strategy when their own sense of alienation and of being cut off as a Cape Bretoner was, in part, a very direct byproduct of the failure of this government to act?
Or if you are one of the 20,000 unemployed auto workers who are in part symptomatic of the reality that the province of Ontario, for the first time in Canadian history, is becoming a have-not province because it has not had an industrial strategy worthy of the name, how are you going to respond to a Prime Minister who talks in very abstract terms today about the need to overcome a sense of personal or regionally restricted grievance? Madam Speaker, it seems to me that you are not likely to respond with a great amount of enthusiasm-if I can put it that way-to the new commitment that we presumably got in the throne speech yesterday.
It is not just the question of a farmer on the prairies, or a potential steelworker in Sydney who is unemployed, or an auto worker in Ontario who is unemployed. There are general categories which the Prime Minister mentioned that I think are more devastating as examples of the reason that we have tension.
The Prime Minister committed himself and his government in 1971 to the view that redistribution of wealth was a hallmark of his party. If it is so, it is the wrong kind of hallmark because during the period he was Prime Minister we redistributed wealth all right, but upwards. After a decade, instead of the poor in Canada being reduced as a statistical entity, their proportion increased numerically.
In 1968, again to deal with the issue that he brings appropriately before us today in his speech, he raised the question of regional development. What happened? In Atlantic Canada both the number of new jobs and percentage of new investment declined in comparative terms with the rest of Canada throughout the decade during which the present Prime Minister governed this country. So we did not get regional development. We got an exacerbation of regional economic circumstances after the present Prime Minister's decade in power.
Similarly in the throne speech concern was expressed about women and inequality. The reality again is that women in our country have, after years of the present government, a large gap between their salaries and those of men because this government talked in abstracts and did nothing about it in ten years. In fact, the gap has widened somewhat not narrowed, in the past decade.
A resource-based economy is indeed central to what the Prime Minister has said, because there are feelings of regionalism in northern Ontario and in much of British Columbia. There are feelings of regionalism in every part of our country that is dependent on resource extraction and export of those resources abroad. These people do not feel they are getting a square deal from Ottawa or from their national government.
A few years ago, in 1968, the Prime Minister said we had to diversify our economy and get away from dependence on the export of resources. Again, the reality is that in 1978, after ten years of Liberal government, our dependence on the resource sector has grown from 51.6 per cent to 54.5 per cent. Instead of making us less dependent, we became more dependent.
I could go on and cite other examples but I will not at this point. The important point about all of these items, as well as
April 15, 1980

the others I could cite, is that not only did the Liberals fail completely to deliver on these worth-while goals during the past decade, but they did so from within the framework of being able to act if they had wanted to.
There are a number of examples, among them inflation and unemployment in general across the country, where a government of Canada is very much influenced by world circumstances; but every one of the examples I have referred to-and they were deliberately selected for that reason-were areas of policy that the Government of Canada could have acted upon and produced measures that would have reduced some of the problems-apart from their inherent justice that the Prime Minister talked about-if it had wanted to act. The reason we have problems in these areas is because the party opposite did not do in 1968 what it promised. So why should we believe them today?
1 want to spend half of my time in this important debate on the question of national unity, more narrowly defined in the sense that I want to talk about the referendum. Before doing so, I want to say something about certain particular items that could get immediate action, but which we have had no sign we are going to get from the present government. We got it in the throne speech and, if I may say so, we got it from the Prime Minister today, a nice general framework. If one is complacent and concerned simply with the intellectual framework of arguments, one might go away very impressed and say yes, there is a demonstration of an understanding in broad terms of our problems.
Politics, however, is quite different from that. Politics requires something other than a broad understanding. Politics requires action to meet the real needs of human beings if you want to get the general results.
What are some of the real problems and sources of regional discontent that bear directly on the question of national unity and are not getting action? Interest rates, of course, is one of them. The Conservative party criticized the Liberals on this question before last May when they got into power. I accept in one sense that if you operate within that philosophical framework, you may change your policy. There are some policies they may have to change and maybe they should be a little more hesitant about making commitments in advance.
The Conservatives promised a low interest rate policy. When they got in, they increased interest rates four times. The Liberals in the most recent campaign blasted the Conservatives for their high interest rate program. Now they are in power and they too have increased interest rates four times. I want to indicate that these problems are not abstract.
I want to deal with the reply today of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) when he asked whether there is an alternative, and I will come to that in a minute. The situation is alarming because not only in Canada but because of the monetary policies of absurd and irresponsible government in Great Britain, and now in the United States, this kind of economic thinking, which I thought went out forever in 1920,
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
is creating the foundation for a major depression on a worldwide scale. That has been widely recognized.
Some hon. Members; Hear, hear!

Just look at some of the indications in our own country. In the logging industry in British Columbia as of yesterday more than 5,000 workers were out of a job, most of them since January. In Saskatchewan today farmers are losing control of their farms, not in high numbers yet but in record numbers for modern times. Young men and in some cases women can no longer go into farming because of high interest rates.
The home ownership situation in our land is now truly calamitous. Once home ownership was a dream for Canadians. In 1980 that dream is turning into a nightmare, and I do not exaggerate. For those who are going to be renewing their mortgages, and most people with mortgages are young families with income levels that qualified them for minimal subsidies in the last few years-I am told there are about 350,000 mortgages coming up for renewal-the average increase in monthly payment is going to be 54 per cent in one year. That is about $200 a month on a typical mortgage, or almost $3,000 a year.
If the government does not act decisively, and not just for those at the bottom end of the income scale but for every Canadian in this mortgage crisis situation, more people will lose their homes in 1980 than in any period since the depression, and any government should be seriously and humanly concerned about that reality.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

I point out to the Minister of Finance that just two weeks ago in Newfoundland for any fisherman wanting to buy a boat the interest rate went up 2 per cent. I understand that with that 2 per cent increase in the interest rate on a 65-foot longliner, a Newfoundland fisherman will be required to catch 250,000 additional pounds of fish just to pay for that increase.
For the first time since the depression credit unions and caisses populaires are having their very existence threatened because of the high interest rate situation. With regard to small businesses, bankruptcies increased 25 per cent in the first two months of this year. The logging industry on the west coast, fishermen in Atlantic Canada, auto workers in Ontario, credit unions, caisses populaires, small businesses and now medium-sized businesses are all under threat because of the absurd interest rate policy of this government, and that means human beings are under threat.
The Minister of Finance asks what can be done. I say to him that Germany, Switzerland and Japan have a low interest rate policy, though as he knows, the rate has gone up somewhat.

In most cases it is about half what it is in Canada. When you have an inflation rate of 20 per cent in the United States and an inflation rate in Canada of 10 per cent,

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Broadbent
you do not have to rely on the old argument that we have to move anywhere near the Americans in terms of interest rate policy because the real rate on return in Canada is higher than in the United States.
I say to the Minister of Finance that I will provide him with a list of economists if he wants to listen to some progressive people, instead of following the move to the right that has taken place in economic circles in recent years. In that way he can learn something from others and do something that is good for the people of this country. One of our spokespersons in this debate will dwell on that issue at considerable length.
Then there is the issue in the throne speech that has immediate consequences, that of controlling Canadian gas and oil resources. I thought it was a misprint when I originally read my text. The Liberals said they would commit themselves to obtaining 50 per cent ownership of our petroleum industry by 1990. What a challenge! What leadership! Every other country in the world with oil resources, such as Venezuela, Mexico and countries in the Middle East, have long since taken over completely their oil industry, and that is precisely what we in Canada should be doing. However, in ten years with the Liberals, Canadians will have 50 per cent. That is the marvellous Liberal approach that I am sure will characterize all of the other so-called progressive points found in the throne speech. The NDP says that ten years is not good enough. We should have virtually total control of our industry in this country within five years, not half in ten.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
Another practical measure is in the farming area. In addition to bringing down interest rates, which would help farmers, a number of suggestions have been made that the government should act on and which would be useful. One was proposed by Environment Canada, pointing out that if we developed our own greenhouse industry like a number of other countries have, we could be using heat from our power plants that is now wasted and save a billion dollars annually in imports of fruits and vegetables. A billion dollars is very important in terms of the effect on our balance of payments.
A particular which received almost no attention at all in the throne speech and which was totally ignored by the Prime Minister today was the fate of more than one million unemployed Canadians. We in this party are not going to stand back, forget, and make them part of a forgotten generation of unemployed. When there are a million unemployed there is a human reality, and there is an economic reality in terms of the lost production of goods and services. Indeed, we need a budget soon which will have its prime focus on creating jobs for Canadians who want to work and not receive handouts.
In short, apart from the nice general framework provided for by the Prime Minister in his argument, he should have given us some visible testimony that he is going to move in dealing with our concerns. He is right that a sense of patriotism or a feeling of national loyalty is dependent upon our own
economic well-being where we happen to live, and if he had provided that kind of commitment for action in his speech today, 1 for one, and many more Canadians, would be considerably happier than we are at this moment.
There are a number of other areas which require serious action by this Parliament in the coming decade. I say frankly that at this point my party is facing these, but there is no easy answer. We are developing policies ourselves, but I want to list some of these because whether we are in the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, the Liberal party or the New Democratic Party, in our parliamentary work in the next few years we should be seriously concerned about the problems which are associated with maintaining a sane and healthy environment for our people in an advanced industrial age.
This country has uranium resources. What kind of over-all policy do we have for the development of uranium, with all its horrific possible implications if we export it for nuclear war? At the same time what can we do with countless nations around the world which do not have the alternative sources of energy which we have?
Then there is the very important question of military spending, which must be of concern to all of us. One of the disturbing events which came up during the election campaign, which is symptomatic of new developments in the relationships between the United States and the U.S.S.R., is the heightening of their tension. 1 for one as a human being am deeply disturbed by the commitment of both the United Statets and the U.S.S.R., to new and massive spending in the military field.
1 am deeply disturbed by reports which are now being put out in both the U.S.S.R., and the United States of America that they could survive nuclear wars. We have to be concerned because just a few years ago in both of those countries-and notably in the United States-there was expression of deep concern about even talking of the possibility of nuclear war. There was appropriate human concern about the holocaust that would be involved. However, the terminology has now shifted, and mililtary people in both those great powers are convincing themselves and, in the documents that they are producing for the first time, are beginning to try to convince their populations that a nuclear war is survivable.
We have to be deeply concerned about heading off that kind of conflict. To say the least, that is a considerable understatement. In that context it is not just the nuclear development that we are concerned about. We are concerned also about the level of military spending as a whole particularly in the context of the problems of the Third World. There was a commission headed by a very distinguished world citizen, Willy Brandt, which completed its report recently. It pointed out the growing inequality between the north and the south, and pointed out in this context the real danger for the poorer part of mankind of the allocation of so much of our resources to armament.
As a Canadian 1 want to illustrate the point because we ourselves are in the process of spending massively in the military field. On the basis of data produced by the Brandt commission I have made calculations regarding the F-18
April 15, 1980

which we are going to be purchasing in Canada. Many members of Parliament in all parties have been concerned that when that decision is made the economic benefits should be shared in the country. That is a reasonable argument, but the relevant question is whether we should be spending money at all at this point in history for that kind of murderous weapon.
For each one of those planes we buy we could, instead, be providing 60,000 tons of rice for people who are starving in the Third World. For the price of each one of those aeroplanes we could be providing 30,000 pharmacies to the Third World, where drugs or medical care of a sophisticated nature are almost non-existent. That is for only one aircraft. Just think what we could be doing if we had a priority other than spending money in the military domain!
1 stress that this is a problem for mankind. It concerns the west, it concerns the east bloc, and the point 1 am making is that there are increasing amounts now being allocated as part of the gross national products in each of the major powers for armaments. Surely it is a time to renew once again major efforts to bring about disarmament for mankind.

Madam Speaker, 1 would now like to broach the subject of national unity, a subject which concerns not only Quebeckers but all of us. I can say that members of my party share with Quebeckers their independent spirit, their national pride and their love for their heritage but if we want these feelings to blossom we need a solid foundation for our two peoples. My party recognizes that Quebeckers have the right to choose freely their political future; the choice is theirs not ours. As far as we are concerned, the constitution must reflect the country's reality; if it no longer does, then it must be changed. Society evolves and political structures must adapt to its evolution. The Canada of the last century must give way to the Canada of the eighties. As a social democrat party, we must first choose the values we want to implement in our society; then we can decide what constitutional arrangements would be best to reach this goal. Here are some concrete examples of these values; the right to live and to work in one's own language, as language is a fundamental aspect of the personality; the right to hold an interesting and stable job; equality between sexes; security for retired people; Canadian control and development of our own resources. And finally, the effective redistribution of the economic benefits provided by our country.
Madam Speaker, because of the ideological changes that have taken place since the sixties, I think most Quebeckers agree now on these principles. Charron, parliamentary leader of the PQ. In his speech, Mr. Charron cited many examples of the mismanagement of what he called "the old regime". I want to tell the Prime Minister that we agree on the following programs of the Parti Quebecois: the income supplement program, the automobile insurance program, the incentive program for small and medium-sized businesses, the nationalization of the asbestos mines, the free access to the Quebec territory for recreation, hunting, fishing and other purposes, the objectives of the language act, the health insurance plan. To us those programs are acceptable. Those are several examples of programs the Quebec government implemented within the federal system. Those are the facts. It is thus possible. Madam Speaker, to change considerably the social and economic structures of the Quebec society within a federal system. You simply have to change the parties, especially if the federal government is social democrat.
For my part, Madam Speaker, 1 do not believe that the answer to the constitutional problems of Quebeckers and Canadians lies in sovereignty-association. Why not? There are many reasons for this. It is obvious that no provincial government will support such an association; there will be a permanent conflict between the two sovereign governments. But in my view and that of my party, there is a basic argument against this concept: It would not be a fair arrangement for the ordinary citizens of western and Atlantic Canada. I would like to explain why, Madam Speaker.
At the present time, Saskatchewan farmers, British Columbia lumbermen and Newfoundland fishermen purchase products manufactured in Quebec and Ontario. They can buy these same products at a lower price outside Canada. These products are now protected by import tariffs and quotas. Western and eastern citizens accept this situation because people in Ontario and Quebec pay taxes not only to Toronto and Quebec City, but also to Ottawa. This is the reason.
The Parti Quebecois wants one without the other. It wants the tariffs and quotas, but it does not want Quebeckers to pay their share to Ottawa. Madam Speaker, 1 would like to ask Quebeckers if they would accept such a situation if they were Saskatchewan farmers or Newfoundland fishermen. I do not believe they would because it would not be equitable. Quebeckers want justice like all other Canadians. Once again, is everyone aware that we can say yes to Quebec without saying no to Canada? I am convinced that English Canada is willing to review its whole position within Canada and to negotiate a new agreement. 1 hope that the present debate will bring us closer to each other. It would be a sad thing if a misunderstanding were to lead to a situation where any agreement would be impossible. There have been inequities in the past. It is obvious. Madam Speaker, that we cannot make up for these inequities, but it must also be said that a lot of progress has already been made in Canada. Much has yet to be done, especially in the areas of economic equality, equality of the sexes, control of our resources and employment.
April 15, 1980

Madam Speaker, together we can build a Quebec and a Canada which will be fair and exciting for everyone, there is no doubt about it.
I would like to conclude by moving an amendment to the motion, Madam Speaker. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House regrets in particular the failure of the government to change the monetary policies in effect since 1975, and to instruct the governor of the Bank of Canada to take immediate steps to lower the interest rate by at least two percentage points."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with deep emotion that I rise to make my maiden speech in this House before such a distinguished audience. I feel privileged, Mr. Speaker, to have the opportunity to address my colleagues from the floor of this historic House which has guarded and preserved the rights and privileges of all Canadians since confederation.
First, I want to tell my constituents in Dollard how much I appreciate the honour they bestowed upon me by electing me as their representative in this House. To all the people of Ville-Saint-Laurent, Dollard des Ormeaux, Roxboro and Pier-refonds, I reiterate my deep gratitude for all the help, support and co-operation they gave me so generously.
I should also like to extend my most sincere congratulations to Madam Speaker for the expression of confidence she received from the House. With the electors from the riding of Laval-des-Rapides I feel honoured that their representative should have been chosen by the House to preside over its business.
At the same time 1 wish to tell my colleagues how pleased 1 am to be with them today and follow in the footsteps of the parliamentarians of today and yesterday who contributed so
The Address-Mr. Desmarais
much to make Parliament what it is today. I am very grateful to my colleagues on this side of the House for their warm welcome. I am looking forward to working with them as a team.

I do not hesitate, Mr. Speaker, to express myself in personal terms in this my maiden speech to this House. Reflections on human feelings, individual sentiments and personal characteristics, in so far as they contribute to a better understanding of individual needs are common to the Liberal traditions which my party hold.
We are living in confusing, discouraging, frustrating times. Rising costs, falling productivity, the incredibly complex organization of big business, big labour and big government have reduced the individual to a quivering mass of doubt and uncertainty. We see the most powerful of the world's nations reduced to helplessness before the threats of a group of terrorists in Iran, and we ask what is the meaning of power?
We see Soviet tanks roll into Afghanistan in a brutal and arrogant takeover of a nation. We watch and wonder at this aggression, and we watch and wonder all the more when retaliation consists of an American threat to boycott the Olympic games. It is an exaggeration to suggest that there is a feeling of helplessness growing among ordinary citizens when they witness the helplessness of a major power.
There is a feeling that somewhere along the line we have lost control. Events have overrun us and developed a momentum of their own. This uneasiness exists in spite of the fact that big business has provided us with ever-increasing wealth. Big labour has made sure that the work force gets its share of economic benefits, and big government has so organized the social structures that, in its role of referee, it finds itself in a position where it must attempt to maintain order and a due proportion in the returns allocated to its important and not always silent partners.

In spite of all those developments, today Canadian citizens are more and more isolated from the powers that be. They are entirely dependent upon government, business and labour superstructures which are the framework of our democratic society. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that the majority of our constituents fall into that category of helpless citizens when dealing with large bureaucracies. Those defenceless taxpayers are but pawns in the power play between the major representatives of the community and they have no opportunity for effective action except for exercising their right to vote every four years. This is a very frustrating situation.
Mr. Speaker, I am far from declaring illegitimate or unacceptable the government business and labour democracies that have developed in our society over the last 50 years or so. Obviously the structural gigantism of government, business and labour is a normal and unavoidable phenomenon in an advanced democratic society, particularly in a country like ours where the people are scattered over a vast territory.

April 15. 1980
The Address-Mr. Desmarais
Modern governments are virtually the only ones able to provide various services such as communications, postal service, welfare and others.

in a society as intricately structured as ours, the difficulties encountered by government in perceiving and resolving the interests of the individual citizens are many and complex. The result is that, from many points of view, individuals today, although enjoying a large degree of constitutional freedom, are nevertheless placed under growing constraints in the conduct of their own affairs.
It is true that political parties and governments throughout the western world, since World War 1 and before, have been preoccupied with the need to improve the human condition. The purpose of the policies and programs to which almost all parties without exception paid lip service was to ensure that the substance of liberty and benefit of freedom in real terms- that is an adequate standard of living with a right to equal opportunity-should be available to all.
Chimeric as such objectives might seem in the light of what is happening in the world today, the true democrat, the true liberal, the true believer in human freedom will not despair. Nor will he ever relinquish the hope of making it possible for all men to enjoy the fruits of the creative society; that is, a society in which leisure to contribute and create is brought about, not by forced unemployment but by an arrangement of working conditions and social awareness, enabling people to enjoy the benefits accrued through an incredibly complex system of worldwide industrial relationships.
That system has now developed to a point where it has reached a peak of efficiency never equalled in history in producing everything except human contentment. In the process we may be in danger of surrendering our heritage for a mess of multinational pottage. It may be this realization which explains the nostalgia movement, the good earth movement and the no-growth movement. But you cannot have no-growth industrially and politically without having no-growth intellectually and morally. The slogan, "Stop the world, I want to get off', is not applicable in political affairs.
Let me say right away that, in the history of this nation, succeeding Liberal administrations, with different leaders and sometimes differing policies and programs, nevertheless have been remarkably consistent in creating the necessary infrastructure to cope with basic human needs of food, clothing and shelter, and, I might add, the additional ingredients of hope for a better tomorrow.

Governments must often take initiatives which should come from the private sector but which the latter is unable to take in due time because of its shortcomings. Let us take, for example, corporations such as Polysar, Eldorado, Panarctic and Petro-Can. Combined with ever-increasing responsibilities in all fields of social activity these types of government initiatives
are such that day by day, the modern state is becoming a terribly heavy bureaucracy which finds it difficult to perceive the needs of the ordinary taxpayer. Big business is motivated by the same demands as big government. Our consumer society has created needs which small and medium-size businesses fail to meet because of the pace of modern living. Consequently, big business tends to spread to all sectors of industrial and commercial activities. In doing so, little by little it eliminates small business, thus forcing an increasingly large number of workers to retrain or to collect unemployment insurance. As with any human structure, commercial firms have always tended to develop into large power conglomerates; very often, these conglomerates tend to withdraw to their ivory towers and therefore to become further and further removed from the people. They become less and less able to recognize the true needs of individuals which they have been entrusted to serve and whose welfare should be their ultimate goal.
The citizen himself is practically prevented, even through his government, from exerting any influence on such large and complex corporations as Exxon, General Motors, ITT and other multinationals whose position is similar to that of city-states in the Middle Ages, that is beyond and outside the effective control of governments. In spite of all the abuse heaped on big business in general and on multinationals in particular, it remains that those corporations, precisely because they are huge, are in a position to meet mass consumer needs while providing a livelihood to millions of individuals.
The substantial growth of those corporations has naturally led labour organizations to become more and more powerful. There is no doubt that, precisely because of their power, labour organizations have contributed to greatly improve the lot of workers, especially in the public sector and among highly skilled trades.
Today, contrary to the situation prevailing some ten years ago, the boss is often at the mercy of the workers. Union members nowadays are part of a labour elite and not only are they in a position to protect themselves, they become as powerful as management.

In spite of this, Mr. Speaker, our producing and distributing system seems to have a built-in imbalance which makes for unequal sharing of these world goods. Production, both in quality and quantity, seems unable to close the enormous gaps which still exist. And gaps are growing as the disparity between the affluence and luxury of the west and the poverty and hopelessness of a major part of the Third World continues to widen.
In our own society inflation is taking away from workers and those on fixed incomes many of the economic gains which they won over the years. Canadian workers, among the most skilled and highly trained in the world, have seen hard-won gains siphoned away by run-away inflation. Perhaps this is the price we must pay for some phases of social security development. This fact alone makes it incumbent on governments to
April 15, 1980

reduce to a minimum, short-sighted, extravagant, wasteful and non-productive programs which are too often aimed at securing the allegiance of the electorate, rather than contributing to a healthy economy. We, as individual citizens, pay a heavy price for the organizations which we have put in place to deliver the goods and services our society requires.
Recently I listened with admiration and respect as the leader of the Quebec Liberal party spoke in the Assembly on the crucial issue of Quebec's place in Canada. That speech was a model of lucidity, of calm and temperate argument, of forthrightness and honesty of which all Canadians can be proud. I am sure that you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that when he spoke of his love for Canada, of his roots in this country and of the roots of all Quebeckers, and when he said that the attachment of Quebeckers to Canada was "visceral", it was difficult indeed not to be moved by the sincerity of his patriotism. May I say that 1 share those sentiments, as I am sure does every Quebec member in this House.
Sometimes as one considers the dark and terrible problems hovering over the world, one cannot help but think that we in Canada, regardless of the language in which we express ourselves, are indeed fortunate. At the same time we recognize the existence of individual dissatisfaction, anxiety, dislocation and anguish among both young and old. I attribute these reactions to the phenomenon of depersonalization and institutionalization which is so much a part of our lives.
On a world scale, it would appear useful to review the highlights of the report of a commission headed by Willy Brandt, former chancellor of the Federal Republic of Germany. This report, representing years of independent study by 18 world leaders, was submitted to the Secretary General of the United Nations, Kurt Waldheim, on February 12, 1980, and is entitled, "A Program for Survival".
The picture is one of a world in which the economic system of production, distribution is progressively breaking down.
Starvation, inflation, disorder, escalating unemployment, international monetary confusion, competition for energy, food, and raw materials, increasing population, advancing deserts, overfishing and pollution are some of the horrors described in this authoritative document.
Let us look at some of the specifics. In the western world there are 18 million people out of work. This unemployment is largely located in countries where a subsistence level is required in order to purchase food and provide shelter and heat.
Irreversible destruction of the ecology is taking place in a number of countries, many of them ranked among the world's poor nations. Deforestation is going on apace, and present world wood stocks will be cut in half by the year 2000. World population is growing by one million every five days. There will be two billion additional people to feed in the next 20 years, and there are 800 million below the subsistence level today.
The Address-Mr. Desmarais
In the affluent society of the west, each person consumes 100 times as much energy as people in the poorer countries of the Third World.
These are among some of the more chilling facts in the Brandt report. 1 do not cite them in order to impress or stun the House, but merely to show the powerful and cumulative impact of the failure of our system to reach those in greatest need.
The Brandt report makes a powerful appeal for a tough, hard-nosed and realistic approach involving, it is true, sacrifices on the part of the west. Better enlightened sacrifice now than chaos later!
The Brandt report calls for a world summit to consider a massive transfer of funds to developing countries, an international energy strategy, a global food program, and reform of the international monetary and financial system.
All of these proposals are worth serious study, and 1 am sure they will receive that study from the dedicated men and women at the head of our affairs. I know that the very gifted and knowledgeable Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is aware of these initiatives and has them under study at the present time. We all recall his notable participation as the chairman of a world conference on north-south problems.
There is also a proposal for an oil strategy to guarantee supplies and prices in the world, and I am sure this is being studied with interest by the responsible minister.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, please let me emphasize my concern regarding our complex and massive institutions. Our institutions have become more powerful and egocentric than ever before. Governments, business, and labour all vigorously defend their point of view without realizing that they are doing so at the expense of the two-thirds of our population which happen to be unorganized. As a result our citizen is progressively losing his battle to shape his own destiny.
1 submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is a major objective of modern government, after basic needs are met, to create conditions in which the individuals, while retaining control over his identity and personality, can devote his leisure time to creative activities in arts and culture.
When one thinks of the golden age of the Renaissance, or the Victorian age in literature-a period when writers, artists, composers, architects, engineers, scientists, competed in excellence in Europe and America-these periods stand out for the productive use of leisure. Certainly, along with the Elizabethan age, as A. L. Rouse has written, they represented societies that were both dynamic and creative.
It is a fact that our society faces important problems in the economic and fiscal areas and in the areas of international relations and internal cohesiveness. We must address ourselves to problems of the economy and problems of internal unity.
I am confident that by skill, patience and understanding, these problems will be overcome and Canada will march into a new era or progress. But we must know where we are going and how we are going to get there. In the field of energy, we

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Desmarais
must conserve, we must develop new sources of energy and we must diversify. I am confident that these things will happen.
1 recall that when the United States refused to join Canada in building the St. Lawrence Seaway, Louis St. Laurent said Canada would take the initiative, and we did. Today, we face equally important and challenging decisions with regard to getting energy to market-Bay of Fundy tidal power, northern gas pipelines, moving clean, pure water from the northern watershed to the water-starved cities of the eastern seaboard. To the resolution of these challenges we must bring the same kind of enlightened and patriotic daring that motivated Prime Minister St. Laurent 30 years ago.
Returning to the creative society, our country can do a great deal more to support art and culture than we have ever done. We can do more to bring out into the sunlight of public acclaim the cultures of other races than English or French; the many races who settled in Canada bringing with them the cultural dynanism of the old world. These we must recognize and accept, and to them we must accord the kind of recognition that will result in a new and vibrant form of social expression.
Thomas Jefferson saw the key problem of the modern world, the problem of the individual. A more ancient book said that man does not live by bread alone. Individuals require the social buttressing that comes from institutions that are progressive and flexible, with clearly spelled out and agreed upon purposes. Individuals require also to live and work in a cultural context with which they are familiar and which contributes to their spiritual well-being. When people sense that they are participating in a society that is creative and dynamic, then they are aware of social and spiritual well-being. Great works of art, architecture, ballet, theatre, and yes, triumphs of engineering, help to overcome the depersonalization of institutions and the constraints applied to individual self-expression.
What is modern man to do, Mr. Speaker, faced with the bigness, impersonality, declining standards, self-serving policies, and waste of many modern institutions? I strongly believe that the human personality is crying out for the opportunity to redeem its own soul. Is this too far-fetched? Are humanity and integrity becoming permanently submerged by our mass institutional imperatives?
Henri Bergson wrote "II faut a l'homme un supplement d'ame"-something to satisfy the spirit. Without this, in the long term, our affluence, technology, our GNP and our prosperity will become increasingly irrelevant.
In the sixties our own young people rejected the values of the corporatist-military state, along with much of its affluence. Today, many of the values of the western world, our acquisitiveness, our greed, our unconcern and disdain for human perspectives, our fatal death wish which sees us polluting the environment with reckless disregard-all of these are totally repulsive to the older civilizations of the Third World.
It is our particular function, in line with the findings of the Brandt report, to establish priorities between technology and human values; between scientific accomplishments and the
preservation of the human soul-that is man's capacity to preserve his individual integrity and order his own destiny.
In essence the issue is whether the social structure will be designed in accordance with the needs of the many or simply to perpetuate the tyranny of the few. Whether we are speaking of government tyranny, the tyranny of the media, the tyranny of great corporations, or merely of the all enveloping tyranny of mediocrity, the final result is the same.

Even if we have failed to develop fully this potential of human freedom which we hold so dear, we are witness to the horror of enslavement that is steadily gaining ground in Communist totalitarian countries. All eastern Europe is under the Communist yoke. In Africa, some Communist governments remain in power with the help of Russian tanks and Cuban guns. In Southeast Asia, the idealists who looked upon the Viet Nam war as a war of liberation recognize with terror that their worst fears are coming true. The almost diabolical strength of Russian communism has now caused a genocide unequaled since Hitler's.
President Lincoln once said that the United States could not survive with half of the population reduced to slavery. Men of good will must now recognize that the world cannot survive with one-half of its population free and the other half enslaved, and that Russian communism is behind this cloud of slavery which is spreading over the world.
In pursuing its goal, nothing can stop the U.S.S.R., and the sad situation of the people in Afghanistan is only one example. As a matter of fact, it can truly be said that man's right to exercise his freedom is more threatened than it ever was in the dark ages. Mr. Speaker. I am afraid that we are on the brink of a new dark era where the freedom of man will become a pale light in an ocean of darkness. I feel it is our duty, to the extent that we believe in freedom and democracy, to keep that light shining. Fortunately, there are still signs of hope.
During the recent election in Rhodesia, we were struck by the moderation shown by the black leader, Joseph Mugabe, in dealing with the white people in his country. Let us hope, Mr. Speaker, that the same moderation will be the key, one of the solutions to our problems, instead of building on fear and hate, as the Marxists do, that man has opted for moderation and compromise, and is urging the whites of Rhodesia to share in the development of the African society in a new spirit of dignity. Mr. Speaker, that is the course to follow.
Specialization has enabled us to channel our efforts quickly in new fields of endeavour. As John Donne said, "No man is an island", we can say the same without hesitation about our governments. They must apply themselves to understanding what is going on in the world, apply themselves to defining the objectives to be pursued and finding the means to achieve them. Our survival depends, Mr. Speaker, on our capacity to adapt to the major changes forced upon us. Our decisions must be taken in the light of those changes.
April 15, 1980

Allow me to express once again my concern for the citizen as an individual. Allow me to suggest to the governments that they take time to consult and listen to the citizens and their institutions to get a better idea of where the priorities lie. Freeing the human spirit is the ultimate goal of all social activities. Creativity is at the very basis of all social achievement. The importance of human contribution to our decisionmaking process must be reaffirmed. That is the characteristic of a creative society and the aim 1 recommend to our leaders in all spheres of human activity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to congratulate you and Madam Speaker on your appointments to these very important positions in the House.
Since this is my maiden speech in the House of Commons, I would like first to take this opportunity to thank the voters of Peterborough riding for sending me to Ottawa as their representative. It is less than a year since I first entered federal politics and already I have been involved in two rather quick repetitive federal elections, quicker than I would like to have seen. However, I am grateful for the support 1 have received from my colleagues in the House. I am also grateful for the support that I have received from members opposite because it was due to their policies that 1 was able to gain this seat.
There are a number of reasons why 1 am proud to represent the constituency of Peterborough. Mine is only one of 282 ridings in the country, but all other constituencies would be hard pressed to match the physical beauty and the quality of the Kawarthas. With a population approaching approximately
100,000	people, Peterborough county is the gateway to the Kawartha Lakes, one of Canada's prime tourist attractions. Two-thirds of my constituents live in an urban environment and most of those are located in the beautiful city of Peterborough. Many of the remaining one-third farm some of the best agricultural land in Ontario.
Mine is a riding like few others in Canada because within a ten-minute drive of the huge General Electric plant in downtown Peterborough are some of Canada's best lakes, finest fishing and most beautiful parks. My riding is also one which realizes how essential it is to look after its young people. Our educational system is second to none and includes an excellent elementary and secondary school system as well as Sir Sanford Fleming College and Trent University. To the young people in my riding I send my sincere appreciation for their support in the past election.
The issues in Peterborough county are the same as in most ridings with a rural-urban population mix. More than 72 per cent of the homes in Peterborough county are owned by the occupants. That figure is well above the Canadian average of 62 per cent and the Ontario average of 63 per cent. As a result, many of my constituents are gravely concerned about the current levels of high interest rates.
The Address-Mr. Domm
Because of the Kawartha Lakes and the importance of tourism in the Peterborough area, environmental issues are also in the front rank. Two environmental issues in particular, acid rain and Eurasian milfoil, pose grave threats to my riding, as they do to other parts of Canada, including British Columbia. I will be directing many of my efforts in this House to these two areas, the economy and the environment.
In many ways Peterborough has been fortunate as Canada enters the 1980s. After several years in the economic doldrums during the mid-seventies Peterborough began to perk up in 1979, and last October unemployment hit a five-year low. Employment in the major industries, particulary at General Electric which employs over 4,500 people, has been very encouraging.
The people of Peterborough are also looking forward to the arrival in our city of the Parks Canada regional office from Cornwall. Although the new government has been reconsidering the move, economic common sense dictates that the transfer be carried through. It was work researched by the Liberal government and acted on by the Conservative Parliament. Because of its more central Ontario location, Peterborough riding is much better suited to serve the province of Ontario than the present location of the regional office in the southeast corner.
I remind hon. members that there seemed to be very little objection to the Quebec branch of Parks Canada moving out of Cornwall and going to Quebec. As well, to serve the interests of national unity and to meet the needs of the Francophone employees of Parks Canada office personnel, the two school boards in Peterborough county have already made plans to introduce Peterborough's first French-immersion program. All in all, it bodes rather well for the future of our country. At a time of the referendum vote I find it very encouraging that the government has seen fit to move Parks Canada to Peterborough, and Peterborough in turn has seen fit to introduce French immersion for the Francophones.
As a relative newcomer to the House 1 would not make my maiden speech without commenting upon impressions I gained during the short Thirty-first Parliament. Although our time in power was brief I feel we did accomplish a great deal. When the Progressive Conservative government of the Thirty-first Parliament is remembered and written about by the historians, it will be because of the two major issues of the 1980s, that is to say, energy and the economy. Perhaps our defeat on February 18 might be compared to the case of the patient who switches doctors because he does not like the diagnosis.
In hindsight many have said that we should not have introduced such a tough budget and that we should have offered more in the way of goodies. That may have been good politics but it would not have been what this country needed.
It is interesting that shortly after the February election, President Jimmy Carter announced massive changes in the 1980-1981 American budget. His proposals included plans for a ten cents a gallon excise tax on gasoline; spending cuts of some $14 billion; a 20,000-person reduction in the civil service, and the first balanced budget in the United States-at least in

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Domm
the last 12 years, or as long as I can remember. When 1 first heard the thrust of the Carter budget I got the feeling that perhaps we had lost the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), that he might have moved to Washington and his budget had turned up disguised as President Carter's antiinflation program.
I cannot say strongly enough how proud I am to be associated with this party. The leadership shown by the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) and his cabinet during the Thirty-first Parliament and the winter election campaign, makes me very confident about our new role in the Thirty-second Parliament. We can hold our heads high. We told the people how it was. We told them that the free ride was over and it was time to address the major problems in our economy today, problems like high interest rates, inflation and deficits, and how we proposed to deal with those things.
Members opposite felt it was time to bring down that government. They felt they had alternatives they would like to present. 1 say to them that they are absolving themselves of all responsibility in the financial management of this country if they neglect to bring in a budget within 60 days. 1 feel very strongly that you cannot stand in the House of Commons day after day, week after week, and month after month, and tell us as opposition and critics, which is our role, that you are not going to introduce a budget for another several months.
i wish I could say I had the same feelings of confidence about the new government that I had about the last government and their financially accountable budget. The throne speech we heard this week offered absolutely no help for the thousands of Canadians suffering because of the current interest rate crisis. Perhaps the clearest comment on the speech was in the reaction of the money markets. The Canadian dollar dropped by more than half a cent in value in one day following the speech, as reported in the Globe and Mail.
We in Peterborough have seen the new government's indecisiveness at another level. The minister responsible for Parks Canada, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts), announced on March 12 of this year that he would make a final decision regarding the transfer of the Parks Canada regional office from Cornwall to Peterborough within ten to 14 days. The first deadline passed on March 22. The second deadline passed on March 26. It is now April 15. Maybe the minister is too busy. Maybe he is indecisive. Maybe he cannot make up his mind. Maybe he has not had enough study in seven years with regard to where Parks Canada should be located.
The fact is that neither the minister nor his colleagues can make a decision. This is important, and not only to Peterborough. It is important to the people of Cornwall and those families who have moved to Peterborough and are commuting to Cornwall in order to do their job. The employees affected by the lack of decision-making on the part of the government are 20 families who have already purchased homes in Peterborough, plus approximately 125 families in the process of deciding where to enrol their young people in school. In addition, accommodation has been acquired in Peterborough and the building is vacant awaiting a decision by the minister. Many civil servants and their families are living in a town at the cost of the taxpayers of Canada with no job to do. The vacillation shown by the minister in this matter was an indication of what we could expect from the Liberal government at the opening session of the Thirty-second Parliament.
My constituents are also very anxious and concerned to hear about another government decision which it is having a great deal of difficulty making. It will affect the Peterborough riding. This decision is with regard to the constituency of Durham-Northumberland. That constituency was recently the victim of a horrible natural disaster when flooding caused millions of dollars of damage to the town of Port Hope. Last summer Eldorado Nuclear, a federal Crown corporation, announced it would construct a $100 million refinery in Hope township near Port Hope just south of Peterborough.
Last summer the new Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-1 do not see him in the chamber this evening-announced that for the time being he was going to stop the progress affecting the construction of Eldorado Nuclear.
Last month, Eldorado Nuclear Limited, a federal Crown corporation, announced it would construct a $100 million uranium refinery in Hope township near Port Hope.

Last month the new minister decided to review that in the same way the ministry is reviewing Parks Canada. He made that announcement at the same time as the town was digging out from the $10 million damage caused by the flood. He made that announcement despite the flood, despite the impending closure of the Firestone Canada plant in nearby Whitby, and despite the fact it will cost $24.5 million more to construct the refinery in northern Ontario, as well as an additional $3 million in operating costs to build it in the north.
I would like to know why such a decision would be made at a time when unemployment is 2 per cent higher in Port Hope than in northern Ontario and when $3 million has already been spent on site preparation in Hope township. Common decency says a community should not be kicked while it is already down. I urge the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Lalonde) to allow the project to proceed in Hope township as common sense dictates, as Liberal research indicated, and as Conservative action proved.

On another level, I am curious as to what steps the new government will take to help those affected by the current high
April 15, 1980

interest rates. The throne speech was long on generalities but very short on specifics as to how interest rate problems will be handled. Considering that the program the Conservative party put forward for mortgage interest deductibility was attacked for nearly a year by the Liberal party-not all, some liked it and some voted for it-I would like to know exactly what it intends to do to help Canadian home owners.
We were told by members opposite that our mortgage deductibility plan would help the rich. However, it is now estimated that thousands of these Canadian rich people might lose their homes. It is interesting to read some of the comments made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) when sitting in opposition during the last Parliament. I will quote what the Liberal minister said in this House last November. He said that "approximately 400,000 families must renegotiate their mortgages after the interest rate has risen by close to four percentage points. We are facing a lot more bankruptcies and defaults; that is what we are facing." He asked what the government was going to do about it.
I trust the new government will remember these comments made by the minister at that time and that it will take action to reduce interest rates, or at least figure out a way to give assistance to home owners, not the rich, but the 400,000 people the minister said will be affected.
The new government should be condemned for approving the Bank of Canada's new method of determining interest rate increases. It is a blatant arrogant method of abrogating responsibility.
It is also interesting to recall some of the comments made by the hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) while he was opposition critic in the last Parliament. I again go back to last November. The Liberal minister said, "The Liberals and 1 generally want action taken now to prevent the hardship this Conservative high interest rate policy is creating for millions of Canadians and their families". As I said, these interest rates have risen more than 2 per cent since the election of the new government, and we are still waiting to see what action will be taken to help the small businessman, home owners and farmers. Let all Canadians see what specific actions the government now intends to take. Let us see what is planned. We asked in the question period today what the government might propose and when it might propose a new budget. The answer was a flat "no" to the end-of-May date given.
When I first decided to seek election to the House two years ago, I did so as a businessman and a consumer who was provoked by what years of mismanagement had done to the economy of this country. I was ashamed that thousands of Canadians were out of work, that federal spending was out of control, and that the federal government was building up huge deficits year after year. I was disgusted that inflation was eating up the savings of Canadians in my riding and across the country. I believed last December, and I still believe, that during his term as minister of finance the hon. member for St.
The Address-Mr. Domm
John's West put the economy of this country back on the right track.
I still think we have to reduce and eliminate the huge federal deficits before we will ever come to grips with the twin problems of inflation and high interest rates.
I was disappointed with the statement in the throne speech which downplayed the importance of reducing the federal deficit, and I disagree completely with the assertion that Canadians do not want less government. That is what it says in the throne speech. The ministers in the new government certainly have not yet figured out exactly what the people of Canada are saying. They are saying they want less spending, less government, less inflation, and less interest. Of course we want more effective government, but that more effective government also goes hand in hand with trimming away the fat and reducing the size of the civil service.
To my mind the federal government in the past decade has taken on all the characteristics of a giant octopus, with its tentacles reaching into every part and corner of the country, sucking every dollar and every cent out of the people in business, stores, on farms, in counties, cities and high rise towers in Toronto and Montreal. What is it all for? Is it really necessary for a government to get this involved in the lives of Canadians? 1 just wonder how this country would have developed at all if the explorers and settlers who opened up Canada had to dodge piles of Statistics Canada and tax forms, or cross mountains of regulations or rivers lined with bureaucrats.
As I mentioned earlier tonight, one of my prime concerns and one of the major issues affecting my constituents in the Peterborough riding is the matter of acid rain. The minister of the environment in the last Parliament, the Thirty-first Parliament, the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), recognized the problem of acid rain as one of the most serious problems which has ever faced our country. I hope that the new minister will take the same approach. If we as a Parliament do not start to take measures to deal with acid rain soon, we will leave a horrible legacy of lifeless lakes for our children.
It is a frightening prospect that our lakes and fishing and tourist industries, all the things which are so vital and important to my riding and to many other ridings in Canada, are damaged, and ignored by the present government in its throne speech as it addresses the subject of environmental protection, which is completely absent from the throne speech. It is even more alarming that the ability of the soil and the crops we grow and the forests could also be impaired if this insidious problem is allowed to continue unabated.
The hon. member opposite who spoke just before me, giving his maiden speech, talked about millions and billions of people, "deforestation" and the cost and the necessity of food, and 1 say that with acid rain falling on us at its present rate of 11 ounces an acre we will have major problems in supplying our own food and our own forest industry if we do not address the subject and present legislation to control effectively the acidity fallout that is affecting our lakes, trees, forests and plant life.

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Domm
The joint Canadian and American study on acid rain released last fall indicated that some lakes in the Haliburton-Muskoka area of south central Ontario have already lost from 40 per cent to 75 per cent of their acid neutralizing ability in the past decade.
In addition-and this is scary-there are 140 lakes in Ontario, mostly in the Sudbury area, which are already acidified at the present time. They are dead to life, dead to fish, dead to plant life, and dead for human consumption.
The problem is not limited to Ontario because similar results are turning up in the maritime provinces, the United States, western Europe, Scandinavia, and Japan.
Acid precipitation threatens to get worse as oil prices cause electrical utilities to turn to coal to produce electricity. The costs to begin to combat acid rain are going to be tremendous. During the last Parliament we in this House heard that it will cost Canadians between $350 million and $500 million annually over the remainder of this century just to bring about a 50 per cent reduction in sulphur dioxide emissions in eastern Canada. Similar estimates in the eastern United States run as high as $7 billion annually. That is a lot of money, but 1 remind the House that the forest product industry in Canada is a $17.5 billion industry, and we have to protect that industry. We learned the lesson in Scandinavia ten years ago of what will happen if we do not put the necessary programs in place to purify the air and to purify emissions before we have acid rain fallout.
Even though that sounds like a great deal of money-and indeed it is a great deal of money-we in this House have to remember that there is more at stake here than just hard economics. The real issue is our lakes, our people, and the kind of future we are going to provide for our children. The real issue is the survival of our environment as we know it today. This is an issue which crosses party lines, and 1 ask that the Minister of the Environment give it top priority as he pursues his duties.
Another major issue in my riding-and with this one I would like to close my remarks on the throne speech-and one that may become important in many more ridings, is that as of next year metrication is again going to take flight. We in Peterborough had the misfortune to be chosen as one of the three test areas for the implementation of metrication in our stores. I do not like to sound facetious, but I wonder if the people of Sherbrooke and the people of Kamloops enjoyed the honour of being guinea pigs as much as we in Peterborough did.
Of course the Metric Commission, in its infinite Liberal wisdom, chose to begin metrication in the retail sector in Peterborough at the height of our tourist season when thousands of Americans and Canadians are visiting and passing through the riding on their way to the Kawartha Lakes.
During the last Parliament the Conservative government appointed an overview committee to study metrication and, following its recommendations, the conversion process was postponed for at least a year. Now it has been announced that
the process will continue early next year in over 20 cities in Canada. The point of the delay was to give Canadians a chance to debate the merits of immediate metrication, a chance they never had, and as the Conservative minister of state for small businesses, the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington), said after announcing the postponement last December, there was little urgency for proceeding immediately because the metrication program in the United States was seven to nine years behind that of ours in Canada.
My only question is: why the rush, why not give Canadians a chance to debate the issue, why force metrication on the people of Canada when there are three cities where the results of that forced metrication could be reviewed? The result is disastrous.

If this Thirty-second Parliament refuses to listen to the people of Canada, refuses to respond to their wishes to have their day in court, to have that moment of trial here in the House of Commons, there might be disastrous results. Maybe everyone opposite likes the metric system. Maybe all of us on this side have some things we like about that system. But what is the point of being ten years ahead of the United States? What is the point of implementing a form of metric measure that is foreign to most in the world?
What is the point of implementing the metric system in Canada when only 4 per cent of our export market, including Germany, is on the metric system? Germany is still buying four-by-eights, and so is Japan. The wood should fit your home when you instal it. What is the rush? The metric system has never had its day in court and Parliament has never discussed it. Never has a piece of legislation come through this House which has said that the government wants the metric system to be adopted in Canada.
I say to the new government-and I hesitate to call it the new government because this is the old government with the same, tired ideas-review the metric system before its implementation.
Let me say in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that I hope this is not another example of Liberal arrogance with which we became so familiar during the Thirtieth Parliament. We want answers to fight inflation. We want answers to cut government spending. We want to reduce the size of the bureaucracy. We want to get the interest rates in line with what people can afford. If the government will not listen, it will be held accountable and an election might come about sooner than any of us would like to see it.
