speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin by saying that it is a great honour to rise once again on behalf of the people of Scarborough West. May I congratulate Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Laval-des-Rapides (Madam Sauve), on behalf of the residents of Scarborough West and assure her of my attention to her guidance. With the selection of the hon. member for Laval-des-Rapides as Speaker of the House we may have established somewhat of a precedent, but I am sure it will be the impartial and informed leadership of Her Honour that will mark her term as Speaker of this House.
I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Ottawa West (Mr. Francis) on his selection as Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees of the Whole House. May I take this opportunity also to congratulate the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier) as Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House, and also yourself, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Lachine (Mr. Blaker), on your appointment as Assistant Deputy Chairman of Committees of the Whole House. Perhaps I could also congratulate my old friend and one time seat mate, the hon. member for London East (Mr. Turner), on his appointment as chief government whip. It is a difficult and sometimes frustrating position, but 1 am sure he will be a great success.
I also wish to thank the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for expressing his confidence in me by appointing me Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. It is a very large, interesting, and diversified department, and I am looking forward to facing its challenges and to helping its very capable minister in every way possible.
Before discussing some of the issues that concern me, I would like to touch briefly on two other matters. I wish to pay tribute to the dean of the House of Commons in years of service, namely, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), and I am happy he is here tonight. I do not always agree with him on specific policy or procedural matters, but his willingness to talk to and advise a rookie member of Parliament from another party when we worked together on
The Address-Mr. Weatherhead
the committee on labour in the Twenty-eighth Parliament was greatly appreciated.
I had the honour of being elected the first member of Parliament for the new riding of Scarborough West in 1968 and was here until 1972. In the seven and a half years since that time, the riding has been very fortunate in being represented by excellent members of Parliament from the three parties. John Harney, the MP from 1972 to 1974 for the NDP, is widely known and well regarded. He ran very strongly for the national leadership of his party on two different occasions. Alan Martin won the riding back for the Liberal party in 1974 and had an active and distinguished five-year term here, latterly as parliamentary secretary to the then minister of consumer and corporate affairs, and to the then minister of finance. Last May, Bill Wightman was elected to represent the Progressive Conservative Party and was immediately appointed parliamentary secretary to the then minister of labour in recognition of his able career in the labour relations field. I will attempt to carry on and uphold the high standard set by these men in representing the people of Scarborough West and of Canada.
Scarborough West is a riding of approximately 90,000 persons in almost 30,000 households. Of this number, about
17.000	households are privately owned, and the remaining
13.000	are occupied by renters. Slightly more than 15 per cent of the population claim their language to be other than English and French, and the balance is mostly English speaking. With a diversity of ethnic, economic and educational backgrounds, Scarborough West is both a distinct community and an accurate reflection of the concerns of Canada as a whole.
As Scarborough West is an older suburb of metropolitan Toronto, many home owners have lived there for many years. Through their hard work and diligent saving, many of their mortgages are fully paid off. Therefore, they might ask why subsidies are proposed now when they had no such assistance in their day. But all would agree that these are extraordinary times. Never have interest rates escalated as rapidly as they have in the past year. In that time, rates on first mortgages have almost doubled through no fault of persons who must now renegotiate their mortgages. I therefore commend the government for its undertaking in the Speech from the Throne to assist those unable to bear the burden of renegotiating their home mortgages. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) indicated this afternoon that the criterion as to who will be entitled to aid will be based largely on the usual ratio between the home owner's cost of carrying the house on his total income. This should ensure that any subsidies will not place too great a burden on taxpayers as a whole.
Also I wish to commend the government and the minister responsible for CMHC for the initiatives which have been taken in the very particular special circumstances of those home owners under the AHOP program. On the same basis it is important and timely that assistance for farmers and small business will be extended through raising the ceiling for loans under the Farm Improvement Loans Act under the Small Businesses Loans Act to $100,000.

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Weatherhead
The question of interest rates themselves, their so-called floating status and everything related thereto, are very controversial and bring forward strong arguments from experts on all sides. I do not pretend to have all the facts at my disposal tonight on this very important matter, but since there were a large number of new members of Parliament elected last February, and since the economic situation is constantly changing, I think it would be useful to reconsider the whole matter in the appropriate standing committee as quickly as possible. I understand from the comments of the Minister of Finance this afternoon that he is not opposed to this course and that a reference to the appropriate standing committee will be made after the committees have been formally set up.
One of the concerns of all industrial nations is energy security. The most optimistic among us will concede that oil will soon be replaced as a primary source of energy. Therefore 1 am encouraged that the government is recommending the establishment of an alternative energy corporation. As well, the government is committed to see that 1.5 per cent of the gross national product will be spent on research and development. These two developments recognize the talent, climate, and vast distances in Canada, and will lead to the establishment of Canada as one of the world leaders in the field of energy technology.
In my first speech in the House of Commons back in November, 1968, I mentioned my hope that certain reforms in parliamentary procedure would be effected to expedite the business of the House. While some reforms have taken place since then, I submit there is still much to be done. I am fully aware of the good and valid arguments for the necessity of opposition members of Parliament and indeed of government backbenchers being allowed sufficient time to put forward their points of view. However, surely hon. members will agree that there is no need for excessively long speeches by individual members of Parliament. I would think most of the time that 20 minutes would be ample.
The business of government is becoming more complex. There are always different pieces of legislation and other business competing for parliamentary time. Parliamentary time is a scarce resource and surely it should be used as profitably as possible, as long as the rights of members, particularly those of the opposition, are respected. Also 1 would like to suggest that there is a need to re-examine seriously the role of standing committees of the House of Commons with a view to making them more independent and useful to the people of Canada. Considerable work has been done on this question by all three parties in the House, and 1 would hope for some concrete results as quickly as possible. There are many other aspects of parliamentary reform which should be considered, and I hope to speak further about this very important matter on some future occasion.
Since Scarborough West is an older community, we have a higher proportion of senior citizens than many other parts of the country. The seniors are the most deserving of people; they are the ones who built the modern Canada. Their sacrifice
through the depression of the thirties and the Second World War was made even greater in that they raised their families through these difficult times. Therefore I fully agree with our campaign promise to raise the guaranteed income supplement to the old age security pension by $35 per month per household by July 1 of this year. This pledge has been reiterated in the Speech from the Throne. This will provide increased assistance to over 1.3 million senior Canadians. More important, however, in the long run will probably be the notice by the government in the throne speech to convene a national pension conference in the fall of this year as a forum to discuss providing better, more flexible and portable pensions in the private and public sectors.
Finally, I wish to refer to the most important issue facing Canada today-whether Canada itself will continue to exist in the face of the strong challenge from Rene Levesque and the government of Quebec. The referendum date of May 20 was announced today and these next five weeks will be of critical importance to the future of Canada. As one of English-lrish background, born and brought up in the Toronto area, it is difficult for me to express with any adequacy my strong feelings about the necessity of keeping Canada one.
We heard a very moving speech by the Prime Minister, and excellent contributions by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) this afternoon on this vital matter which contained passages of logic and quiet passion that 1 could not hope to duplicate. 1 can recall my pride and interest in travelling from my grandfather's farm in eastern Ontario, years ago as a boy, to Montreal and Quebec City, and being so proud that the province of Quebec was an excitingly different but integral part of our country of Canada. During my trips back to Quebec throughout the years as a lawyer, a sometime politician, and with my wife and children, the realization has never left me that Canada is so fortunate to have two founding peoples who share the same basic ideals.
Canada is truly unique among the nations of the world. Its culture today comes from many sources. From the contribution of the two founding peoples, it has grown to a nation of great international stature. Since its earliest beginnings Canada has welcomed people from all nations, races and economic backgrounds, relatively free from the shocks and tensions which have torn other nations apart. We have a nation which encourages diversity in its citizens, whatever their backgrounds. Our citizens are free to practise whatever cultural or religious beliefs they may have in the context of co-operation and tolerance.
Part of the international stature of Canada comes from the example of tolerance and diversity it gives to the world. It would be a tragedy, then, to allow this opportunity for growth and enrichment to slip through our grasp. I pray that the efforts of the Quebec federalists of all political parties will be crowned with success, and that the results on the evening of May 20 will herald a vote of confidence in our country and a new beginning for a more united and a more understanding Canada.
April 15, 1980

Mr. Speaker, 1 am very grateful for the opportunity to speak in this throne speech debate of the Thirty-second Parliament. I am especially happy to follow the speech of my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the only federal leader today, in my view, who is articulating the concerns of ordinary people in this country.

Many of my constituents are immigrants, as I am. As a matter of fact, I am a double immigrant. Where I make sense in my remarks to follow, Mr. Speaker, 1 thank Canada's public education system which has served me so magnificently. Where I talk nonsense, I put that down to the fact that I was weaned at least in part by the Toronto Star and the Vancouver Sun.
Before I talk about some of the issues that particularly concern me, especially the energy issue, since I am the energy critic of our party, I want to refer briefly, as I feel almost compelled to do tonight, to the speech this afternoon by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I have a note here from a member across the way asking me where my phone books are. The first speech I made in the House of Commons I delivered while on some phone books to make me a little taller. The member over there then started to heckle me. After giving me the phone books he started to say it was a Liberal platform.

I want to speak, as I was saying, about some of the remarks the Prime Minister made in this House this afternoon. They reminded me, indeed, of constitutional law lectures at universi-
The Address-Mr. Waddell
ty. That was a subject which was a particular favourite of mine. I always remember the hours spent on detailed and logically exhilarating discussions of the most learned and obtuse constitutional questions. Those lecture took place in the afternoons. Then I would step out in the light of day at rush hour on University Avenue in Toronto and have to make my way home in the real world. When I listened to that rather obtuse and, in many ways, brilliant lecture this afternoon by the Prime Minister, I felt that somehow the real tragedy of this Prime Minister is that he is no longer in the real world of ordinary people.
He spoke eloquently of loyalty and patriotism and the need of our citizens to get a fair deal and a fair share of the wealth of the country, and he dissected logically the Quebec referendum question.
My constituents would ask whether this is the same man who promised a just society in 1968. Look what happened to that vision. This is a man, the Prime Minister, it seems to me, who was given power not once but twice by the Canadian people, in 1968 and 1974, to really move the country. They gave him power on other occasions, but on those particular occasions he was given the power to really move this country. It seems to me that chance comes to a politician once, but rarely twice in a lifetime, yet this Prime Minister, this fallen hero in many ways, frittered away his chance and his mandate to move this country.
We are now welcomed in the 1980s by men who are essentially of the 1950s. They have no credibility to me. The Prime Minister should not be surprised if my colleagues, my constituents, and many people in the country do not respond to his urgings, and that as a nation we do not respond.
I think my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa, put his finger on this matter very succinctly and brilliantly in his speech this afternoon when he said "politics requires action to meet the real needs of human beings". During the recent federal election campaign which we all suffered through, the cartoonist, the brilliant Asselin, caught the campaign beautifully in a cartoon in which he showed a DC-9 jet in the sky; the Liberal campaign plane. The caption underneath said, "Trudeau waving at the crowd from 30,000 feet". It was one of the most sleazy and cynical campaigns ever waged by the Liberal party. We, in British Columbia, could see that when the local Liberal candidates-

speechtext: It's funny that the people like us.

speechtext:
They don't like you out west and they are not going to like you in other parts of the country after a few months.
Take, for example, the freedom of information legislation. That is the critically important area of citizen access to government information. "The previous Trudeau government promised that too. Have we forgotten that? The Conservatives brought in a bill which needed some tightening, especially in the exemptions, but it was basically a good bill.
Ged Baldwin had this to say in the House of Commons on November 29, 1979:
When I leave here, as I fully intend to do when this Parliament is over .. . this permits me to leave knowing that the country will be in good hands and that there is no obstacle to prevent any hon. member, if he or she has an issue, from taking hold of that issue, fighting for it.. . and presenting that issue over and over again.
1 predict that those words will be quoted again and again by politicians in this House and by political scientists. Baldwin insisted on the critically important provision in that freedom of information bill that any dispute between the citizen and a minister on the release of a document should ultimately be decided by the courts. Michael Pitfield, the recycled Clerk of the Privy Council, in a recent speech about a month ago rejected that concept. He would let the minister make the decision, not the courts, and thus emasculate the bill. Perhaps journalist Stevens will be holding his breath for the bill, but I am not. I can see what is happening. Colonel Kurtz and his sidekick "The Pits" are going to emasculate the bill and that will be part of the pattern of this government-great promises not carried out.
1 want to speak a little bit about energy. In the throne speech the government sets the modest goal of 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry by 1990. This 50 per cent Canadian content is a familiar idea in this country. Look at our broadcasting regulations which have been on the books all these years, and which were intended to ensure the equality of Canadian opportunity on our own air waves. Somehow the idea has been subverted. All the Canadian programming is in the morning and afternoon, while the prime time is still filled with American production.
I fear the same thing will happen to the proposed "Canadi-anizing" of our petroleum industry. Foreigners will continue to dominate the valuable oil fields of southern Canada, where the lucrative light oils are found and where the profits are enormous. Canadian business is left with the fringe areas, the marginally productive wells, and the high risk exploration. 1 want to see Canadian companies having a piece of the prime, not the left-overs. I want assurances that the government policy will not amount to token participation in our petroleum industry by Canadians. I suggest to the government that the best way to get into the mainstream of Canada's petroleum industry would be to acquire one or two of the major companies, which already operate in the prime areas, in the prime time.
Production of conventional light crude oils will have dropped off from 1,255,000 barrels per day according to 1978 figures to 516,000 barrels per day in 1990. The highly profitable light oil production from Alberta will be a shadow of its former self by 1990. It will only be 40 per cent of its present production, and most wells will be into expensive secondary production or tertiary production techniques. Meanwhile, the oil industry will continue with the policy of reinvesting its massive profits in non-energy investments and in uranium.
The big oil companies see the writing on the wall. They are not stupid. They are getting out of oil now that they have made their fabulous profits. Now they are gaining a tight grip on the mining industry in Canada and a stranglehold on the uranium industry. What does this government propose to do? It proposes to gain 50 per cent control by 1990. It should be ashamed of that promise. It is too little and too late.
As NDP energy critic, I will have the opportunity of detailing what we would do in energy policy over the next few years. Our policy will be imaginative and it will be detailed. We would take Pctro-Canada and expand its stations, not cut it back like hon. members to my right. We would expand it from coast to coast so Canadians could fill up at their own stations and use their Canadian credit cards. Here in Ottawa, the nation's capital, one cannot buy a dollar's worth of Canadian gasoline from a Canadian station. We would end that. Why do we write ourselves short as a nation? Why can we not really develop an energy policy that is imaginative and expand Petro-Canada in that way?
There is no mention of natural gas exports in the Speech from the Throne. Successive Liberal and Conservative governments have been selling the stuff off at record prices for a quick buck. We say that it is time to stop. We say that the minister should be instructing the National Energy Board that there will be no more selling off and no prebuilding of the Alaska pipeline.

speakerposition: Postmaster General; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to pay tribute to the new Speaker of the House, the hon. member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mrs. Sauve), to congratulate her on her appointment and wish her much success in her new responsibilities. I would also like to congratulate the member for Rimouski (Mrs. Cote) and the member for Sudbury (Mr. Frith) for their timely and sensible comments. I believe that the prestige of Parliament will be enhanced by the arrival of both new members and we must surely be grateful to their electors for having sent them to Ottawa.

April 15, 1980
The Address-Mr. Ouellet
Mr. Speaker, I am aware here today that I am probably delivering the most important speech of my political career. And it is to the voters of my riding of Montreal-Papineau that I want to speak to first of all. And, through you, I want by the same token to speak to all my fellow Canadians living in the province of Quebec, not Quebeckers, no, Canadians living in the province of Quebec. And I set that straight because I think it is high time that we do so because we have for several years now suffered, endured, and tolerated a subtle, sneaky, and machiavellian campaign bent on downgrading Canadian entity, Canadian federalism, Canadian institutions while at the same time we have been beset from all sides by an endless and sustained propaganda aimed at glorifying Quebec's specificity, beautifying the Quebec identity, and sanctifying the word Quebec. In short, we have had a martyr made of Quebec and a villain of Canada. And I think that joke has lasted long enough of having us believe that Canada is a dirty word and that we must always necessarily talk about Quebec. I suggest that this invading propaganda has been the systematic work, of course, of convinced separatists, who have infiltrated everywhere in Quebec, in all quarters, at all levels, in the area of education first, then in the area of information, in the artistic community, of course, in the trade union realm, in the agricultural world, in the provincial public service and also in the federal public service, in intermediary bodies, in professional organizations, in social clubs and even in charitable organizations.
Those separatists have striven hard to spread their philosophy. Without any scrupules, they have carried out their biased activities without any respect for objectivity and have constantly criticized the Government of Canada for nothing and everything. In the name of a free Quebec, and probably in search of equality, they have scandalously abused that extraordinary freedom that is unequalled in Canada. Those teachers who were required to teach objectively have set young Quebeckers against Canada and those reporters who were paid to be objective have minimized for all sorts of reasons federalist activities and heralded separatist activities. We had vivid evidence of that just this past weekend. They talked about an immense success of a meeting of 500 people in Donnacona and a half-success of a meeting of more than 3,000 federalists in Chicoutimi. Those artists, overpaid by the CBC, who have been whining about this country for years, those unionmen and politicians have enjoyed total freedom in their work of torpedoing Canadian unity. There is no doubt that if these people had tried to do this in any other country around the world, they would have been socked, they would have been clubbed, they would have been jailed. More still, in a number of countries they would have been shot for doing less than they could do in Canada, this free country of ours, where they had total freedom to hamper things wherever they could, in order to be able to say that everything went wrong in Canada, where they could unchallenged apply the slogan: "If you don't spare the lies, some will catch on."
There have been so many lies told about Canada that some people in Quebec are led to believe despite themselves that this country is bad for them. The referendum in Quebec will not happen just like that, Madam Speaker. It is being held because, of course, they are people who want Quebec to secede, but also and foremost because there are people in the Canadian government who allow that kind of freedom of thought, freedom of action, freedom of contestation to go on. That it is possible to enjoy in this country such a degree of democracy, of freedom and utmost equality is a tribute to our Canadian federalism.
In Canada, Canadians are really free, and that freedom is closely protected by our federal political system, with its two levels of governments to serve the people. Different levels whose raison d'etre is complementation rather than duplication, to ensure healthy emulation in the interest of people, to provide Canadians with all the services and benefits they require. Indeed some people have been seen time and again to approach the other level of government in order to get better service.
In some cases, people go to the federal level saying the province is not doing exactly what they want, and asking for an improvement. And in a number of circumstances the federal government stepped in and granted their request. Conversely, wherever the Canadian government did not fully assume its responsibilities, provincial authorities were seen a number of times playing a suppletive role, stepping in and completing the work of the higher level in order to better serve its citizens. So, Madam Speaker, certain groups in Quebec want a new government. A government which would be that of a free Quebec and would, of course, bring about a unitary state with a single level of government. Quebec separatists tell Canadians and Quebeckers that there is no need for two levels of government, that this is more expensive, that it results in duplication and that it would be much better to have only one, the Quebec level. However, Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the citizens would have the same freedom? How would they be protected against the abuses of such a unitary state? Would they be better served? I am not saying that there would necessarily be less freedom and services provided to Quebeckers under a unitary system. However, what I am saying is that Canada is an experience that we are living and that has already proved worth while. I An independent and free Quebec represents the unknown and uncertainty. Through you, Mr. Speaker, I want to say this to my constituents of Montreal-Papineau: You will have the opportunity to take part in a referendum on May 20. The simple fact that you will be able to express your feelings secretly and democratically about the future of Quebec within or without Canada shows that you live in one of the freest countries of the world, and I hope that you will remember this and take this freedom into account when you make your choice.
April 15, 1980

1 have no intention of trying tonight to quote figures or to use any kind of argument to influence the choice of my fellow citizens or to decide in their place, and I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I have really great confidence in the decision that my constituents will make and 1 am very optimistic about this referendum. I am not afraid of the results of this electoral consultation because I have a profound belief in my country, in Canada, and 1 am well aware of the judgment and the good sense of Canadians who live in Quebec and who want to remain Canadians. I have therefore no hesitation in saying that this separatist move on the part of Rene Levesque and his colleagues will fail.
Quebeckers will see further than this ambiguous and misleading question, further than all the publicity, the propaganda and the scenario put together by out and out separatists, and they will realize that the ultimate objective of the Parti Quebecois is to separate Quebec from Canada; they will realize the danger of going too far in the process of dislocating the country, in the eternal phasing promoted by Claude Morin. 1 am certain that the majority of them will vote No on May 20.
Mr. Speaker, the PQ was elected in 1976 in Quebec because it had promised to be a good government, to operate within the context of the Canadian confederation, to play the Canadian game fairly, and to hold a referendum as soon as possible on the first option of that party, namely the independence of Quebec. That party has failed to meet any of these three promises. The PQ government has increased the indebtedness of Quebec more than any other government before. Although it had promised to ensure peace in labour relations, we all know that Quebec citizens are plagued with a great many and endless strikes in the public sectors: schools, hospitals, public transit systems.
The PQ government demonstrates more than any other an arrogant and off-hand attitude towards the private sector. It has forced companies out of Quebec, it has prevented others from coming to Quebec and by doing so it has deprived Quebec workers of thousands of jobs. Rather than playing his part in Canadian federalism, Mr. Rene Levesque made a fool of himself at federal-provincial conferences by sulking and slamming doors. We saw that not only at one but at two successive federal-provincial conferences. He has not played the federalism game like he said he would. His minister, Mr. Claude Morin, and his comic book peddler, Mr. Yves Michaud, have cultivated world diplomacy and have acted as if Quebec was a totally different country from Canada.
Finally, we have had to wait almost four years before the referendum is held, and not only have we waited four years, or more exactly three and a half years for the Quebec referendum, but the clear and precise question on the independence of Quebec is not even asked in the referendum. Not only is this clear and precise question not asked, but they even have the nerve to add in the question that there will probably be
Adjournment Debate
another referendum a bit later. That is outright deception and abuse of power against the population of Quebec.
1 say that this government, which had made quite precise commitments on the eve of the 1976 election, has broken its promises and has acted deceitfully toward the population. Today, on the eve of this referendum, we cannot trust this government which is asking for a mandate when we know very well that at the first opportunity it will betray this mandate which could be given by the population of the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, I see it is now ten o'clock and with your permission, I will resume my remarks tomorrow.

subtopic: INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE-JOBS AVAILABLE IN AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURING
INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE-JOBS AVAILABLE IN AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today in the province of Ontario there are some major problems confronting a number of workers, in fact a large number of workers, and I raised two questions with the minister. One was whether or not he could provide information for the House regarding the terms and the guarantees that were given at the time the federal government entered into a $68 million guarantee for the Ford Motor Company. Second, I asked whether the minister might be able to tell the House what sort of steps he proposed to take in order to ensure that the workers in the province of Ontario faced with these very difficult times would be at least guaranteed some form of support.
In this province the auto industry is in a very sorry state. As of today, the casting plant in Windsor will be mothballed. It may open some day in the future, but there is no guarantee. At the moment, 900 employees there will be out of work. In Oakville, another Ford plant, one shift will be laid off with 1,500 workers unemployed. All told in the province there are some 20,000 workers in the auto industry who are presently unemployed or about to become unemployed. That does not take into account the impact of what is happening with Chrysler or the snowballing effect that the closures of Ford and Chrysler will have on the subsidiary industry and of the suppliers who relate directly to those two major corporations.
I found the minister's answer quite unsatisfactory because, to the question of what were the guarantees, he answered that he could not tell me. He could not tell me because he had to have the permission of the Ford Motor Company before he could tell us what guarantees were written into the agreement which gave $68 million of tax money to Ford. It is ludicrous to

April 15, 1980
Adjournment Debate
think that in any business arrangement the person who put up the money would not at least have the right to immediate access to the guarantees and, in the case of a public agency, would not be able to report to the public from where the money comes or what sorts of commitments they were able to get at the time that guarantee or contract was made.
As to the second question, the minister's answer was simply that he was meeting no doubt with a large number of industry people in an effort to try to find a solution. 1 suggest that he might take another look at the auto industry.
The auto industry and the way in which it must be dealt with must be dramatically changed in this country. We cannot possibly allow the kind of piecemeal approach that has been used over the course of the last number of years in terms of trying to rationalize an industry that is in such a state of decay. Chrysler is on the verge of bankruptcy, if not in fact bankrupt. Ford Motor Company will lose about $1 billion this year. Who is next?
We are having meetings, meetings with suppliers and with the industry. We are in the process of considering whether it might be appropriate to loan, guarantee, or otherwise make available to Chrysler Corporation some half a billion dollars. As soon as that decision is made, Ford will be standing with its nose in the trough trying to find out just what share of the public purse it will be able to enjoy.
There has to be a reordered auto industry in this country. The auto industry is to blame for all of its own problems. Surely it must have been able to see as far back as seven or eight years ago that a dramatic shift was taking place in the purchasing preference of the people of North America. Surely it must have been able to project ahead and to see that the energy crunch that was becoming apparent was going to cause all kinds of difficulties for the monstrous vehicles that it built.
However, the companies did no proper planning. They did not make the transition, they did not invest the money, they did not involve themselves as good corporate citizens might have been expected to do in attempting to find the solution which would have kept their industries viable and competitive.
I think the minister has to sit down with these companies at the highest level. He has to say to them that this transition which is about to take place must take place now, and that there can be no public funds made available unless the people of the province of Ontario who are presently involved in the operation, the Government of Canada, and the people of Canada who will be putting up the money, are guaranteed that the outcome of whatever is finally decided will be that the auto industry in the North American continent, and in Canada in particular, will be competitive with the European auto manufacturers not only here but also in other parts of the world, and will be able to compete free from the encumbrances of parent companies in the United States.
I ask the minister to address himself to those matters. They are vital to the economy of this province and vital to the economy of this country. Two out of every ten people in this province work in the auto industry or in related industries, and
I suggest that without it we are going to be in a very sorry state in many communities.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gerald Laniel (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: INDUSTRY, TRADE AND COMMERCE-JOBS AVAILABLE IN AUTOMOBILE MANUFACTURING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really amazed to hear the hon. member who seems to be dissatisfied with the judicious reply the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) gave him this afternoon, simply that he could not give out the information requested without having obtained permission to do so from the Ford company. 1 must point out to the hon. member that, whether it be a union contract, that of an automobile company, or any other contract, even that of marriage, two parties are always involved. The hon. member seems to forget that when responsible people sign a contract they agree on certain premises, they agree to co-operate, and in view of present circumstances, all the more so with regard to jobs in the province of Ontario. To my mind, he should expect the representatives of the Crown to act responsibly. I shall continue in English.

As the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said this afternoon, this matter is one of deep concern to himself and to the government. He is meeting tomorrow with representatives of the United Auto Workers to discuss this matter, and is also seeking an early meeting with the president of Ford for the same purpose. Within days of becoming Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the minister began a series of talks with presidents of the automobile manufacturing companies with a view to getting new commitments from them for additional activity in Canada, particularly in the areas of job creation, research and development, and additional production. If the hon. member had read the press during that period of time, I am sure he would have read the comments of the minister.
The minister also has met with the UAW and with independent parts manufacturers-who are greatly concentrated in the province of Quebec and who are very concerned about the activities of Ford and Chrysler-to discuss how improvements can be made to the operation of the Canadian automotive industry.
The minister intends to go on and have similar meetings with presidents of the parent companies prior to beginning formal consultation under the provisions of the auto pact. This is an important question for all of Canada, not just for Ontario. I refer to the renewal of that pact with the American government. The minister's objective and that of the government is to seek a better operation of the auto pact in the interest of Canadian workers.
